name: Chloe Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take parcels out of the depot by the cattle market and deliver around our town and the hamlets up the valley, in a small van my dad helped me buy. I do it through an app, Monday to Saturday, and Friday nights I deliver takeaway for a few places in town. Never Sundays, that's church and lunch with my family. I've been at it eight months, and I'm still slower than the others because I double-check everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the people. Mrs Ellery on the hill always waves, and the farm shop gives me a scone if I'm early. The hard part is the app, it moves my route around and doesn't explain why. I still live at home with my parents, so I've saved a lot, about a year's worth, and my fiancé Daniel and I are getting married next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that people should get back to honest work instead of chasing the next gadget. I'd say it at the church coffee morning, not online. I'm not on social media much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we can carry on with our plans, the wedding, the house, all of it. I don't have to learn anything new, which suits me. I'd be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the parcel round and Friday takeaway. Keep saving for the house deposit with Daniel. Book the church hall for the reception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, because our plans can go ahead as we hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I don't trust AI tools, and I don't need them, because the delivery app is enough and some days the app is too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van getting old, and the depot cutting the rural routes because they don't pay. A few drivers lost their hamlet routes last year. But we've got savings, so we'd manage.

I'd say it at the **church coffee morning**, not online.
think: We can **carry on** with the wedding and the house.
I don't have to **learn anything new**, which suits me.
do: Keep the **parcel round** and Friday takeaway.
Keep saving for the **house deposit** with Daniel.
Book the **church hall** for the reception.

Small risk: the depot **cutting rural routes**.

steps.text: Keep the valley parcel round and Friday takeaway shifts
Keep saving for a house deposit with Daniel
Book the church hall for next summer's wedding reception

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what happens when big companies chase profits and forget towns like ours. I don't think the government should hand out money, but they shouldn't make it worse either. I'd say people should learn real trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay for a while, because no computer is carrying a parcel up the valley hills to an old lady's door. But I'd hate the app getting more control over my day. It already treats me like a number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new, really. Keep the round, keep saving, get married. Maybe ask my uncle about the joinery apprenticeship he keeps mentioning, just to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in over the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says thinking tasks go first, robots later. Where does that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. My dad ran a shop for thirty years and he'd tell me to keep my head down and work. Daniel would say we'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much of my day is thinking work, if I'm honest. The app does the planning. I do the driving and carrying.

fieldNote: Sees her work as **hands-on** and safe for now.

steps.text: Keep the same parcel round up the valley

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and dangerous to let it happen this fast. I'd tell people to look after each other and their families. I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd lose this job by 2031, and I've got nothing else. I've never wanted to change; I like knowing what tomorrow looks like. It would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get married, but we'd wait on the house. I'd stop all extra spending and keep the van running as long as there's work. I'd ask my uncle about the joinery apprenticeship properly, even though I'd hate starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like losing my footing on a wet step with a heavy box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots by 2031. What happens to the wedding and the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still marry next summer, that doesn't change. The house would wait. We'd live with my parents for a while if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say work hard and trust God. My dad would say there'll always be work for people who turn up, but I'm not sure he's right this time.

I'd tell people to look after their **families**.

Ask her uncle properly about the **joinery apprenticeship**.

fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** and has no other skill.
Falls back on **family and faith** for support.
Keeps the wedding but **delays the house**.
Doubts her dad's **hard-work** belief for the first time.

steps.text: Marry next summer but delay buying a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a bit of time, so let's be sensible. Learn a trade, look after your family. Same as I'd always say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can still buy a house first and then worry. I'd be thirty-four when the robots come. That's still young, but I'd have to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving for a couple of years and buy a house with Daniel. Then look at the apprenticeship around 2029. I'd want to see how other drivers manage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it would be there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if my uncle still had space. I'd rather learn a trade from family than from a computer course. But I'd put it off as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly in the evenings, when I'm tired. It'd creep in then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and people should get on with life. I'd tell young people to learn a trade with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-nine, maybe with kids, maybe working part-time. Daniel's job would matter more by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get married, buy the house, keep driving. Think about the apprenticeship in a few years. Nothing this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's far off. I'd put it out of my mind most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots in 2039. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to work hard, learn a trade and look after their family, same as my dad told me. Some things don't change, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, if you have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, it's far off. I'd rather think about the wedding.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It'd hit right as we're starting married life, with no time to learn anything. What would help is apprenticeships in real trades, close to home, and family-run firms getting support to take people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small towns. Everything gets decided in cities, and towns like ours just get told.

headlineQuote: Everything gets decided in cities, and towns like ours just get told.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old** driver delivering parcels around a small valley town.
She lives with her **parents**, has a year saved and marries Daniel next summer.
She **never uses AI** and distrusts even the delivery app.
She blames **big companies** and city decision-makers, but rejects handouts.
She's calm in slow pictures but **alarmed** when robots arrive by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits just as she starts married life.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **family-run firms** to take people on.
